before.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark questions on radiation risk and benefit, the mark scheme rewards evaluation: you must identify the specific benefit in the given scenario (what the radiation does and why it helps), identify the specific risk (which type of radiation, which cells are at risk and why), then reach a justified conclusion. Simply listing “benefits: cures cancer; risks: causes cancer” will not score highly — you need to explain the science behind each point and weigh them against each other. The ‘Suggest’ command word means you should apply the science to the context given in the question, not just recall general facts.

Magnification calculations are reliably examined. The most common mistake is using different units for image size and real size — always convert to the same unit first. When asked to ‘explain’ how microscopy has improved our understanding of cells, the examiners want you to use causal language: state what the technology allowed scientists to see, then explain how this changed or extended the scientific explanation (model). Listing microscope types without linking them to specific discoveries will not score the highest marks.

In questions about stem cells and ethics, examiners want you to distinguish between scientific arguments (evidence about what stem cells can do, risks of rejection or tumour formation) and values-based arguments (beliefs about when human life begins, moral weight of potential cures). If you merge these, you lose marks. Always name the type of stem cell you are describing — ‘stem cell’ alone is insufficient. For the mitosis misconception: state clearly that DNA replication happens before mitosis, during interphase. Do not say DNA doubles ‘during mitosis’.

The motor effect and Fleming’s left-hand rule are Higher tier only, so skip this tip if you sit the Foundation paper. For questions on Fleming’s left-hand rule, always identify all three quantities (force, field, current) before answering. A common mistake is using the right hand instead of the left — Fleming’s left-hand rule is for the motor effect. For ‘Suggest’ questions about increasing the force on a conductor, link each suggestion directly to the equation \(F = BIl\) — examiners reward causal language, not just lists.
